8. Response shapes: rca `summary/ranked_hypotheses[cause,confidence,evidence_refs]/blind_spots/suggested_next_checks`; evidence layer names (`failing_result`, `metric_trend`, `sibling_checks`, `upstream_pipeline_run`, `check_history`, `kind_detail`); "hypothesis that cites none is dropped; if none citeable the invocation fails"; sql gen `{sql, explanation}`; suggestions `{suggestions[expectation_type,name,rationale,config,dimension,fail_threshold_hours], rejected, coverage_warnings}`; "if all fail the invocation fails"; `coverage_warnings` = near-miss trigger bindings.

1	# AI features (LLM)
     2	
     3	DataQ can call a language model **you choose** for three jobs: turn a sentence into a
     4	custom-SQL check, propose a starter set of checks for a table, and explain why a check
     5	failed. All three are **off until an Admin configures a provider**, every call is recorded,
     6	and no raw row ever leaves your deployment. This page shows each one with what goes in, what
     7	comes back, and what the model is never shown.
     8	
     9	<video class="clip" autoplay loop muted playsinline poster="../../assets/videos/configure-llm.jpg">
    10	  <source src="../../assets/videos/configure-llm.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    11	</video>
    12	
    13	*Admin → LLM provider: point DataQ at a model, press **Test**, save. Here it is a local
    14	Ollama server; the same form takes Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock or any
    15	OpenAI-compatible endpoint.*
    16	
    17	## Turn it on
    18	
    19	**Admin → LLM provider.** Pick a provider, enter the model name and (for OpenAI-compatible
    20	endpoints) the base URL, paste the API key, and press **Test** — it makes one tiny call and
    21	reports the model and latency without saving anything. Then **Save** and switch on *Enable
    22	outbound LLM calls*.
    23	
    24	![The LLM provider panel on the Admin page: provider, model, base URL, API key, structured-output mode and the enable switch](../assets/screenshots/admin-llm-settings.png){ .screenshot }
    25	
    26	*The key is write-only: it is stored in your secret store, never shown again, and never
    27	forwarded if you later change the provider or endpoint — you re-enter it on purpose.*
    28	
    29	| Provider | Base URL | Notes |
    30	|---|---|---|
    31	| **Anthropic** | leave blank | Native structured output. |
    32	| **OpenAI-compatible** | required | Azure OpenAI (`…/openai/v1`), AWS Bedrock, vLLM, TGI, **Ollama** (`http://host:11434/v1`). |
    33	
    34	**Structured output** decides how DataQ gets JSON back. *Native* uses the provider's own
    35	schema or tool-calling support; *Prompt-JSON fallback* embeds the schema in the prompt and
    36	repairs one parse failure — use it for small local models. Either way DataQ **re-validates
    37	every response** against the same rules a human's input would face, so the mode changes
    38	reliability, never safety.
    39	
    40	!!! info "What the model can and cannot see"
    41	    Every feature below sends **column names and masked aggregate statistics** — counts,
    42	    null rates, min/max, distinct counts — never sample rows. The root-cause narrative
    43	    additionally sends the failing check's observed value, and that value passes through
    44	    the same column-policy and warehouse-tag redaction every results surface applies. A
    45	    column classified as PII reaches the model as a mask. The full transfer-vector
    46	    accounting is in [Security & data handling](../security/overview.md#what-can-move-data-out),
    47	    and the live list for *your* deployment is on the Admin page above the panel.
    48	
    49	## Explain a failed check
    50	
    51	When a check fails, DataQ opens an **incident** and captures an **evidence card** at that
    52	moment: the failing result, the metric's recent trend, the other checks in the same run,
    53	the upstream pipeline run if one triggered it, and the downstream tables that depend on the
    54	asset. You can read the card yourself from the asset page.
    55	
    56	![The incident evidence drawer on an asset: the failing result, expected vs observed values, the metric trend and the sibling checks from the same run](../assets/screenshots/incident-evidence.png){ .screenshot }
    57	
    58	*This card is exactly what the model is handed — nothing is fetched fresh from the
    59	warehouse, so the narrative describes the failure as it was, not as it is now.*
    60	
    61	Ask for the narrative with the incident id:
    62	
    63	```bash
    64	curl -X POST https://<your-dataq-host>/api/v1/llm/rca_narrative \
    65	  -H "Authorization: Bearer dq_live_…" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    66	  -d '{"incident_id": "669964c0-bf09-4e93-960d-7866f7e73b0f"}'
    67	# → 202 {"invocation_id": "5e7c…", "status": "pending"}
    68	```
    69	
    70	The call is queued to a worker; poll `GET /api/v1/llm/invocations/{invocation_id}` until
    71	`status` is `succeeded` or `failed`. This is what a 14-billion-parameter local model
    72	returned for the incident above — a `status in set` check on an orders table where 18 % of
    73	rows carried a status outside `new / paid / shipped / cancelled`, up from 6 % the run
    74	before:
    75	
    76	```json
    77	{
    78	  "summary": "The 'status in set' check likely failed because 18% of the order statuses in the ORDERS table do not match the expected set 'new', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled'. Recent check failures show this percentage rising from 6% to 18%, indicating an issue with order status data integrity.",
    79	  "ranked_hypotheses": [
    80	    {
    81	      "cause": "Data entry errors or updates involving unsupported values have been introduced in the status column.",
    82	      "confidence": "high",
    83	      "evidence_refs": ["check_history", "metric_trend", "failing_result"]
    84	    },
    85	    {
    86	      "cause": "Upstream data sources or processes feeding status values have changed, introducing values outside the allowed set.",
    87	      "confidence": "medium",
    88	      "evidence_refs": ["kind_detail", "check_history", "metric_trend"]
    89	    }
    90	  ],
    91	  "blind_spots": [
    92	    "no upstream orchestration pipeline run is linked — either this run wasn't pipeline-triggered, or none could be matched",
    93	    "no downstream lineage is recorded for this asset — cannot rule out downstream impact",
    94	    "no before/after column profile — profile comparison isn't implemented yet"
    95	  ],
    96	  "suggested_next_checks": [
    97	    "Examine recent changes in data entry practices or source data",
    98	    "Verify if there have been changes in upstream systems providing order status updates"
    99	  ]
   100	}
   101	```
   102	
   103	Three things make this usable rather than merely plausible:
   104	
   105	- **Every hypothesis cites evidence layers** from a closed list (`failing_result`,
   106	  `metric_trend`, `sibling_checks`, `upstream_pipeline_run`, …). A hypothesis that cites
   107	  none is dropped before you see it; if the model produces nothing citeable, the
   108	  invocation **fails** instead of returning an empty story.
   109	- **`blind_spots` is computed by DataQ, not the model.** It lists what the evidence card
   110	  could not see — no linked pipeline run, no lineage — and the prompt forbids the model
   111	  from asserting confidence over those gaps.
   112	- **The narrative reaches the next alert.** Once one exists for an incident, the
   113	  Teams / Slack / email / webhook line for that incident carries its one-line takeaway:
   114	
   115	```text
   116	Incident 669964c0 (status in set) — critical, occurrence 2 · not pipeline-triggered (manual
   117	or scheduled run); 2/3 other check(s) in this run also failing; no downstream lineage
   118	recorded · AI summary: The 'status in set' check likely failed because 18% of the order
   119	statuses in the ORDERS table do not match the expected set 'new', 'paid', 'shipped',
   120	'cancelled'. Recent check failures show this percentage r…
   121	```
   122	
   123	(The clause is capped so a Slack section never overflows; the full narrative stays on the
   124	invocation.)
   125	
   126	The narrative is generated **on demand** and read with the same permission as the incident
   127	(`view` on its suite). It never re-runs the check and never changes the suite.
   128	
   129	## Write SQL from a sentence
   130	
   131	Custom-SQL checks are the most flexible check type and the slowest to author. Describe the
   132	rule in plain language against a suite whose target is a table on a SQL datasource
   133	(Snowflake or Unity Catalog):
   134	
   135	```bash
   136	curl -X POST https://<your-dataq-host>/api/v1/llm/sql_generation \
   137	  -H "Authorization: Bearer dq_live_…" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
   138	  -d '{
   139	    "suite_id": "<suite id>",
   140	    "description": "No order line may have a negative quantity or a unit price of zero",
   141	    "include_profile": true
   142	  }'
   143	```
   144	
   145	DataQ lists the target's columns from the warehouse, adds masked profile statistics if you
   146	asked for them, and asks for **one read-only `SELECT`**. The model's SQL then passes the
   147	same validator a human's custom SQL does — a single `SELECT` / `WITH` statement, nothing
   148	chained after a `;`, no write or DDL keywords — before it is ever stored. The invocation's
   149	`response` has the shape below (illustrative — the SQL is the model's, the validation is
   150	DataQ's):
   151	
   152	```json
   153	{
   154	  "sql": "SELECT * FROM ORDER_LINES WHERE QUANTITY < 0 OR UNIT_PRICE = 0",
   155	  "explanation": "Returns the rows that break the rule; the check fails when this returns any row."
   156	}
   157	```
   158	
   159	Paste the result into the custom-SQL editor like any hand-written query and **dry-run it**
   160	before saving — generation never creates a check by itself. For a rule that spans several
   161	tables on the *same* connection, add `additional_tables` (up to four); cross-connection joins
   162	are refused structurally, because reconciling two datasources is what the
   163	[comparison check](datasources-checks.md) is for.
   164	
   165	## Suggest checks for a table
   166	
   167	For a suite with a table target and no checks yet, ask for a starter set:
   168	
   169	```bash
   170	curl -X POST https://<your-dataq-host>/api/v1/llm/check_suggestions \
   171	  -H "Authorization: Bearer dq_live_…" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
   172	  -d '{"suite_id": "<suite id>"}'
   173	```
   174	
   175	DataQ profiles the table's columns live (masked statistics only), sends the profile with a
   176	**closed vocabulary of check types** — the same catalog the check editor offers — and gets
   177	back candidate checks, each with a name, a rationale and a full config. Every candidate then
   178	goes through the validator `create_check` uses; one that fails is dropped and reported under
   179	`rejected`, and if *all* fail the invocation fails rather than returning "nothing". The
   180	success shape (illustrative):
   181	
   182	```json
   183	{
   184	  "suggestions": [
   185	    {
   186	      "expectation_type": "expect_column_values_to_not_be_null",
   187	      "name": "order_id not null",
   188	      "rationale": "0 nulls in the profile; a key column should stay that way.",
   189	      "config": {"column": "order_id"},
   190	      "dimension": "completeness"
   191	    },
   192	    {
   193	      "expectation_type": "monitor:freshness",
   194	      "name": "order_ts arrives daily",
   195	      "rationale": "order_ts is the only timestamp column; the profile shows a daily cadence.",
   196	      "config": {"timestamp_column": "order_ts"},
   197	      "dimension": "timeliness",
   198	      "fail_threshold_hours": 26
   199	    }
   200	  ],
   201	  "rejected": [],
   202	  "coverage_warnings": []
   203	}
   204	```
   205	
   206	`coverage_warnings` is computed by DataQ, not the model: it lists pipeline trigger
   207	bindings that *nearly* matched this suite (right pipeline, wrong environment) — a gap no
   208	column profile can reveal. Suggestions are proposals: nothing is created until you add them,
   209	so one you disagree with costs a glance. Use them as the first pass on a new table, then read
   210	the asset page's per-dimension coverage to see what they left out.
   211	
   212	## What is recorded, what it costs, who may call
   213	
   214	- **Every call is a row in `llm_invocations`** — kind, requester, suite, token counts,
   215	  duration, the validated response or the reason it failed. The Admin **Test** probe is
   216	  recorded too. Your own invocations are readable by you; all of them by an Admin.
   217	- **Permissions follow the suite.** SQL generation and check suggestions need `edit` on the
   218	  suite; the narrative needs `view` on the incident's suite. There is no LLM tool over MCP
   219	  and no Admin-only feature — an assistant holding your token can do exactly what you can.
   220	- **Rate-limited under its own class**, separate from the REST ceiling, so a burst of
   221	  generations cannot crowd out normal API traffic — and vice-versa.
   222	- **Off is really off.** With the switch disabled, all three endpoints return a clear error
   223	  and nothing is sent anywhere.
   224	
   225	Design record: ADR [0042](../adr/0042-llm-provider-seam.md).

(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

Use proactively when reviewing any PR that touches CLAUDE.md, docs/site/adr/, CONTRIBUTING.md, or docs/site/architecture/overview.md.
